query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys resist simultaneous wear and corrosion in harsh environments because their ability to form a stable, self-healing passive oxide layer minimizes both mechanical degradation and electrochemical attack.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys with a homogeneous microstructure and no pre-existing surface damage.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloys to a combined mechanical wear and corrosive environment.
generation.conditions: Testing is conducted at room temperature in a chloride-rich solution (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) under moderate mechanical loads using cyclic sliding wear.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and maintenance of a stable, self-healing passive oxide layer on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The alloy’s compositional complexity promotes the formation of a protective passive oxide layer that, due to self-healing, dynamically repairs disruptions from wear. This barrier limits both the electrochemical reactions responsible for corrosion and the mechanical surface damage from wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under combined wear-corrosion conditions, alloys capable of forming this stable, self-healing oxide layer will exhibit significantly lower overall mass loss, shallower wear tracks, and reduced corrosion indicators than a matched baseline alloy lacking this robust passivation behavior. In particular, the combined degradation rate will be less than the sum of the individual wear and corrosion rates.
generation.baseline: A matched high-entropy or conventional alloy that does not form a stable, self-healing passive oxide layer.
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold under moderate chloride concentrations, room temperature, and mechanical loads. Under extreme conditions (e.g., very high/low pH, elevated temperatures, or excessive mechanical stress) that destabilize the oxide layer, the beneficial effect may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the synergistic protection is uncertain and may vary with slight changes in alloy composition or testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of high-entropy alloys known to form a stable, passivating oxide layer and a control set that does not. Expose both sets to cyclic sliding wear in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution at room temperature under identical moderate loads. Monitor in situ electrochemical behavior and perform post-test surface analyses.
measurements: Mass loss (quantifying total wear-corrosion damage)
Wear track depth and morphology (via profilometry/SEM)
Corrosion current density or rate (using electrochemical techniques)
Surface characterization of the oxide layer (using XPS/EDX)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy capable of stable passive oxide formation does not exhibit significantly reduced combined degradation (i.e., mass loss, wear track depth, and corrosion indicators) relative to the control, or if surface analyses do not show evidence of a robust, self-healing oxide layer, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the ability to resist combined wear and corrosion in harsh environments is governed by the formation of a stable, self-healing passive oxide film that is promoted by a uniform, nanostructured matrix inherently provided by high configurational entropy.
drafts.material_initial_state: Annealed, homogenized high-entropy alloy exhibiting a fine, nanocrystalline microstructure with an already partially developed passive oxide surface.
drafts.intervention: Exposure to a combined mechanical wear and corrosion environment via cyclic sliding wear in a corrosive electrolyte (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) under controlled load and temperature.
drafts.conditions: Tests performed at room temperature under moderate contact loads within a corrosive medium that is aggressive enough to challenge the passive film but not so extreme as to immediately disrupt it (e.g., standard saltwater conditions). A matched baseline is a conventional alloy of similar elemental makeup but lower mixing entropy and less uniform microstructure.
drafts.structural_mediator: A nanometer-scale, homogeneous passive oxide film that forms and heals along the grain boundaries and phase interfaces of the high-entropy alloy.
drafts.mechanism: High configurational entropy ensures a uniform distribution of alloying elements and results in a fine nanocrystalline microstructure, which together enhance the formation and dynamic repair of a passive oxide film. This film minimizes localized corrosion, while a robust sub-surface microstructure increases surface hardness and reduces wear, resulting in synergistic resistance under combined degradation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under combined wear-corrosion conditions, high-entropy alloys will exhibit lower rates of mass loss, shallower wear tracks, reduced pit formation, and signs of active passive film repair compared to the conventional, lower-entropy baseline alloy.
drafts.baseline: A conventional alloy with a similar elemental composition but with a coarser, less uniform microstructure resulting in less effective passive film formation and healing.
drafts.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold under moderate corrosive and mechanical conditions. In extremely aggressive environments (e.g., high temperatures or very low pH) where the passive film is severely disrupted or in conditions where mechanical stress exceeds the film’s healing ability, the advantage of the high-entropy alloy may diminish.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-entropy alloy samples and matched baseline alloys with similar elemental profiles. Subject both sets to cyclic sliding wear in a controlled tribocorrosion cell using a corrosive electrolyte (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) under identical moderate loads and temperature. Monitor the evolution of the passive film with in situ electrochemical techniques and use ex situ microscopy and surface analysis to characterize wear track depth, corrosion pit morphology, and film integrity over time.
measurements: Mass loss
Wear track depth (via profilometry)
Corrosion current density (via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy or potentiodynamic polarization)
Surface morphology and film integrity (via SEM, AFM, and XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy does not show significantly reduced combined wear and corrosion damage (i.e., similar or worse mass loss, wear track, and pit density) compared to the baseline alloy, or if in situ and ex situ analyses fail to demonstrate evidence of a dynamically healing passive film, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A stable, compositionally induced passivation layer, combined with local atomic-scale lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys, reduces both corrosive attack and mechanical wear simultaneously by inhibiting active surface reactions and impeding dislocation-driven abrasion mechanisms.
drafts.material_initial_state: A series of equiatomic, multi-principal-element alloys (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with homogeneous microstructures and controlled grain sizes.
drafts.intervention: Alter the alloy compositions to systematically vary the extent of passivation-forming elements (e.g., Cr) and local lattice distortion (e.g., by substituting or removing one principal element).
drafts.conditions: Immerse the alloys in a corrosive alkali chloride solution and subject them to sliding wear at moderate contact stress to simultaneously induce wear and corrosion.
drafts.structural_mediator: Presence, continuity, and protective quality of oxide or protective compound layers at the alloy surface.
drafts.mechanism: Combined passivation reduces electrochemical activity at the surface, while local lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion and mitigates mechanical wear, resulting in higher overall resistance to tribocorrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under combined sliding and corrosive conditions, modified alloys with higher passivation-forming element content and lattice distortion will exhibit measurably lower mass loss and reduced corrosion current compared to a baseline high-entropy alloy with insufficient passivation capacity or lower distortion.
drafts.baseline: A high-entropy alloy with standard compositional balance and minimal passivation element content tested under identical corrosive wear conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under moderate loads and corrosion rates typical of industrial applications; under extreme pH, temperature, or mechanical stress, passivation breakdown or excessive deformation may negate the protective effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform repeated tribocorrosion experiments on control and test alloys with varied compositions, measuring real-time corrosion current and post-test mass loss. Characterize the surfaces for oxide film uniformity and mechanical damage.
measurements: Mass loss before and after testing to quantify wear
Electrochemical measurements (OCP, potentiodynamic polarization)
Surface analysis of oxide layer thickness and uniformity via SEM/EDX or XPS
Hardness and microstructural analysis to confirm lattice distortion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys containing higher passivation-forming elements and greater lattice distortion do not exhibit improved simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance relative to the standard baseline, or if corrosion and wear degrade performance equally across all variants, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the formation of a stable, self-healing passive oxide layer that is enhanced by synergistic effects of multi-elemental composition, which suppresses localized corrosion and reduces wear-induced oxide layer disruption.
drafts.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy with a homogeneous microstructure and no pre-existing surface damage.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy to a combined mechanical wear and corrosive environment, such as sliding wear in a chloride-rich aqueous solution.
drafts.conditions: Room temperature, neutral pH, and a chloride concentration representative of seawater (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl).
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation and stability of the passive oxide layer on the alloy surface.
drafts.mechanism: The multi-elemental composition of HEAs promotes the formation of a chemically complex and stable passive oxide layer that resists breakdown under corrosive conditions. Simultaneously, the high hardness and toughness of the alloy reduce mechanical disruption of the oxide layer during wear, allowing it to self-heal and maintain protection against corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The combined degradation (wear + corrosion) rate will be significantly lower than the sum of the individual wear and corrosion rates measured separately, due to the synergistic protection offered by the stable passive oxide layer.
drafts.baseline: The sum of wear and corrosion rates measured independently in the same environment but without simultaneous exposure.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for HEAs with a high degree of compositional complexity and a stable passive oxide layer. It may fail for HEAs with poor passivation behavior or in environments with extreme pH or temperature that destabilize the oxide layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of a high-entropy alloy and a conventional alloy with similar mechanical properties. Subject both to sliding wear in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under identical conditions. Measure the wear rate, corrosion rate, and combined degradation rate for each material.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss or volume loss)
Corrosion rate (electrochemical measurements, e.g., Tafel extrapolation)
Combined degradation rate (mass loss or volume loss in the combined environment)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined degradation rate of the HEA is equal to or greater than the sum of its individual wear and corrosion rates, the hypothesis is falsified, as this would indicate a lack of synergistic protection from the passive oxide layer.

drafts.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys with a higher proportion of refractory elements will exhibit greater resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion due to enhanced microstructural stability and improved mechanical properties.
drafts.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys with varying compositions of refractory and non-refractory elements.
drafts.intervention: Controlled exposure of high-entropy alloys to a corrosive environment while subjecting them to mechanical wear.
drafts.conditions: Testing will be conducted in a simulated harsh corrosive environment with mechanical abrasion applied to the samples.
drafts.structural_mediator: The microstructure of the high-entropy alloys, particularly the distribution and bonding of refractory elements.
drafts.mechanism: Refractory elements contribute to a more stable microstructure that resists degradation from both wear and corrosion mechanisms.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with higher refractory content will show significantly lower rates of wear and corrosion compared to those with lower refractory content, indicating a synergistic effect in resisting both degradation modes.
drafts.baseline: A matched set of high-entropy alloys with lower refractory content will serve as the baseline for comparison.
drafts.boundary: The prediction should hold for high-entropy alloys tested under similar corrosive and mechanical conditions but may fail if the environment is altered significantly or if other alloying elements dominate the degradation process.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of wear and corrosion tests on high-entropy alloys with varying refractory content under identical conditions.
measurements: Weight loss due to wear
Corrosion rate measured by electrochemical methods
Microstructural analysis post-testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with higher refractory content do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear and corrosion rates compared to the baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation of a stable, passivating oxide layer on the surface, which acts as a barrier to both wear and corrosion.
drafts.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy with a homogeneous microstructure
drafts.intervention: Exposure to a harsh corrosive mechanical environment
drafts.conditions: High temperature, high humidity, and mechanical stress
drafts.mechanism: Formation of a stable oxide layer that prevents wear and corrosion
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved resistance to wear and corrosion compared to a matched baseline
drafts.baseline: High-entropy alloy without a stable passivating oxide layer
drafts.boundary: The prediction should hold for high-entropy alloys with a stable passivating oxide layer, but may fail for alloys with unstable or non-passivating oxide layers

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of high-entropy alloys with and without a stable passivating oxide layer, exposed to a harsh corrosive mechanical environment
measurements: Wear rate
Corrosion rate
Oxide layer thickness and composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy with a stable passivating oxide layer shows no significant improvement in resistance to wear and corrosion compared to the matched baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
